title: T/F/NI + Vocabulary: The Art of Making Noise (poziom wojewodzki)

tasks.instruction: Przeczytaj ponizszy tekst. Zdecyduj, ktore zdania (1.1.–1.6.) sa zgodne z trescia tekstu (T – True), ktore sa niezgodne (F – False), a ktore zawieraja informacje niepodane w tekscie (NI – No Information). Nastepnie znajdz w tekscie wyrazy lub wyrazenia, ktore odpowiadaja definicjom podanym w punktach 1.7.–1.10. Wymagana jest calkowita poprawnosc ortograficzna odpowiedzi.
tasks.text:
THE ART OF MAKING NOISE

Almost nothing you hear in a film was recorded while it was being filmed. The dialogue usually was, and the music arrives later from an orchestra. Everything in between - footsteps on gravel, a coat being pulled on, a sword leaving its scabbard, a punch landing - is added afterwards by two or three people standing in a windowless room full of junk, watching the picture and moving in time with it. The job is called Foley, after Jack Foley, a studio employee who worked out how to do it in the 1920s, when sound arrived and nobody knew what to do about it.

The room itself explains most of the craft. Along one wall run the pits: shallow trays set into the floor and filled with gravel, sand, wood, marble, water and snow, which in this trade means a particular kind of crunchy plastic. Along the other walls are shelves resembling the contents of a house cleared out in a hurry - shoes in every size, leather bags, umbrellas, a broken chair kept for the noise it makes, boxes of cutlery, a wooden door frame on wheels with a working handle. Almost none of it is what it appears to be on screen. The classic tricks are famous: coconut shells for hooves, a stick of celery snapped for a broken bone, cornflour in a leather pouch squeezed to give the crunch of walking through fresh snow.

The reason for the whole elaborate business is that reality does not record well. A microphone pointed at a real punch picks up something disappointing and slightly damp. Real footsteps on a real pavement sound thin and distant, because the microphone is not where the audience's attention is. What the artist produces is not the sound the object makes but the sound the audience expects it to make, which is a different thing and generally louder, closer and more sharply defined.

Practitioners are oddly consistent about which part is hardest. It is not the spectacular effects, which are largely a matter of a good idea and a cupboard of props; it is the walking. A character's footsteps have to carry their weight, their shoes, their mood and the surface beneath them, and each one must fall in the frame where the foot lands, within a margin the audience could not describe but instantly notices. Artists talk about performing a character rather than imitating one, and many will watch a scene several times without touching anything before they begin.

Digital libraries were supposed to end all this. Thousands of pre-recorded sounds can be dropped onto a timeline by anyone with the software, at a fraction of the cost of a studio and two specialists. In practice the libraries have made the craft more valuable rather than less, because a sound already used in a hundred other productions carries a faint, unplaceable familiarity that audiences register without knowing why. Streaming services, producing more hours of drama than the industry has ever made before, have turned out to be substantial employers of exactly the skill they were expected to make redundant.

The work remains almost entirely invisible, which is the point. Foley artists say the compliment they value from a director is silence: nobody in the screening mentioned the sound, so it worked. A few have become quietly famous within the industry, and one or two have been the subject of documentaries. But the profession's own measure of success is that for ninety-nine minutes out of a hundred, an audience believes it is simply hearing what is happening on the screen.

items.statement: Most of the sounds in a finished film were captured at the same time as the pictures.
items.explanation: FALSE - 'Almost nothing you hear in a film was recorded while it was being filmed'; only the dialogue usually was.

items.statement: The technique is named after the person who developed it.
items.explanation: TRUE - 'The job is called Foley, after Jack Foley, a studio employee who worked out how to do it in the 1920s'.

items.statement: Those who do the job agree that dramatic effects such as fights are the hardest part of it.
items.explanation: FALSE - 'It is not the spectacular effects ... it is the walking' that practitioners consider hardest.

items.statement: Libraries of ready-made sounds have reduced the demand for this kind of work.
items.explanation: FALSE - 'The libraries have made the craft more valuable rather than less', and streaming services employ the skill heavily.

items.statement: Directors are said to show their approval of the work by saying nothing about it.
items.explanation: TRUE - 'The compliment they value from a director is silence: nobody in the screening mentioned the sound, so it worked'.

items.statement: Foley artists are paid more than the composers who write a film's music.
items.explanation: NO INFORMATION - The text mentions the cost of a studio and two specialists but never compares anyone's pay with a composer's.
